segments.say: Think about the moment you open your eyes in the morning. There is no loading screen. The room is simply there, all at once. The window, the colour of the curtains, the edge of the blanket, the light on the wall. It feels sharp, it feels complete, and it feels like it's happening right now.

But tonight I'd like to gently suggest something a little strange. What you see when you open your eyes is not a live window onto the world. It's something your brain builds, moment by moment, from scraps of light, a few guesses, and a great deal of expectation. And it does this so smoothly that you never notice the work.

That might sound unsettling at first, but it isn't meant to be. This is not a story about your brain failing. It's a story about how astonishingly well it does a job that is almost impossible, and about the small places where we can catch it in the act.

show.sub: Your brain is good at this

segments.say: Here's what we'll explore tonight. Why your eyes are nothing like a camera. Why you never quite see the present moment. Why colour isn't really sitting on the objects around you. Why people can miss a gorilla walking right through a game. How a voice can change what you see. And why pain, time and even taste are, in their own ways, careful guesses.

segments.say: The way we'll do this is simple, and I hope rather cosy.

Most of us carry around a handful of quiet beliefs about how seeing and hearing and feeling work. They feel so obvious that we never question them. Tonight we'll take twelve of those beliefs, one at a time, and hold each one up against what scientists have actually found.

For each belief, we'll look at three things. First, what most of us assume. Then, what the experiments really found, with the names, the places and the years. And finally, what it means for you, in your ordinary day, or in your bed tonight.

And where the science is still uncertain, I'll tell you. Some of these findings are very solid, repeated many times around the world. Others are newer, or smaller, and deserve a little caution. You don't need to accept anything on faith tonight. You only need to be curious.

Let's go back to that morning room for a moment. The light coming through the window is real. It really does bounce off the curtains and the wall and into your eyes. But what happens after that light lands on the back of your eye is where the interesting part begins.

show.cap: The first light of the morning

segments.say: Because what reaches your eye is not a picture at all.

What reaches your eye is light, arriving at different strengths and different wavelengths from every direction. At the back of your eye, a thin layer of cells called the retina catches that light and turns it into tiny electrical signals. And from that moment on, there is no image anywhere in your head. There are only signals, flickering along nerve fibres.

Think about what your brain actually has to work with. Electrical signals. From two small, curved surfaces at the back of your eyes. Projected upside down and left to right, the way a lens always does. And, as we'll see in a moment, full of gaps and blur. From that, your brain has to build a steady, three dimensional, colourful room.

Here is why that's so hard. The same pattern of light on your retina could come from many different worlds. A small coin held close to your face and a large plate far away can throw almost exactly the same shape onto your eye. A white wall in shadow and a grey wall in sunlight can send back almost the same light. The signal alone can't tell you which is true.

show.sub: Many worlds fit the same light

segments.say: In the nineteenth century, the German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz put it in a way that still shapes the field today. He suggested that perception is a kind of unconscious inference. Your brain takes the incomplete evidence from your senses, adds what it has learned about the world, and arrives at its best conclusion, all without you being aware that any reasoning took place. We will meet his idea again later tonight.

So the room you see when you wake up is your brain's best guess about what is out there. Most of the time it's a very good guess, good enough to find the door, pick up a cup, and recognise a face. But it is still a guess, and like all guesses, it can sometimes be wrong in ways that are surprising and rather beautiful.
And that leaves us with a riddle that we'll carry with us all evening.

If your brain is guessing, why doesn't it feel like guessing? Why does the world seem so solid, so certain, so present? You never wake up and think, my brain predicts there is probably a window over there. You just see the window. We'll come back to this at the very end of the night, once we've collected enough clues to answer it properly.

So think of tonight as a slow, gentle investigation. Each belief we test is a clue. Some clues will be about your eyes, some about your ears, some about your skin and your sense of time. By the end, I hope they'll fit together into a picture that is stranger, and kinder, than the one we started with.

You don't need to remember any of the names or numbers. If you drift off halfway, that's perfectly fine. The ideas will still be here another night. For now, just settle in, let your body get heavy, and let your curious mind come along for the ride.
So let's begin with the belief that almost everyone holds, often without ever saying it out loud.

It's the idea that your eyes work like a camera. Light comes in through a lens, an image is captured, and that image is what you see, sharp from edge to edge, like a photograph refreshed many times a second. It's a lovely, simple picture. And as we're about to find out, it is almost completely wrong.

Here's a small test you can try, even with your eyes half closed. Next time you're looking at a page of writing, fix your gaze on a single word. Don't let your eyes move at all. Now, without moving them, try to read the words two lines below. Most people find they can tell there are words there, but they can't actually read them. That small, surprising blur is our first clue.

That blur hints at four things we're about to unpack. Truly sharp vision covers only a tiny area. Everything around it is soft and blurry. Your eyes are constantly moving to patch the picture together. And your brain quietly hides all the seams, so that the whole scene feels sharp, even though, at any single moment, most of it isn't. Let's look at each of those, slowly.
